top.text: Austen wrote major novels before the age of 22, but she was not published until she was 35. The anonymously published Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814), and Emma (1815) were moderate successes, but they did not bring her public fame in her lifetime. She wrote two other novels—Northanger Abbey and Persuasion, both published posthumously in 1817—and began another, eventually titled Sanditon, but it was left unfinished on her death. She also left behind three volumes of juvenile writings in manuscript, the short epistolary novel Lady Susan, and the unfinished novel The Watsons.

history.query: What is the Great Barrier Reef?
history.answer: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching over 2,300 km along the coast of Queensland, Australia[1][3]. It is composed of over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands, built by billions of tiny organisms called coral polyps[1]. It is the largest single structure made by living organisms on Earth and is a World Heritage Site[1][6]. The reef is located in the Coral Sea, off the coast of Queensland, and is protected by the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park[3][5]. It is also an important cultural site for Aboriginal Australian and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and a popular tourist destination[4].

answer:
The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching over 2,300 km along the coast of Queensland, Australia[1][2]. It is dying primarily because of environmental threats, including population outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish and broader ecological stress.

Crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks are a major driver of reef degradation. These starfish can multiply rapidly in warm, nutrient-rich waters and consume large amounts of coral, contributing to the loss of living coral cover[3]. The Great Barrier Reef hosts over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands, making it the most outstanding coral reef system in the world[1][2].

The reef is also threatened by other environmental factors such as rising sea temperatures, ocean acidification, and pollution. While the marine park protects a large part of the reef from damaging activities[5], the combination of these stressors continues to put the reef at risk of dying.

top.text: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, composed of over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands stretching for over 2300 km (1,400 mi) over an area of approximately 344400 km². The reef is located in the Coral Sea, off the coast of Queensland, Australia.  It is separated from the coast by a channel 100 mi (160 km) wide in places and over 200 ft (61 m) deep. The Great Barrier Reef can be seen from outer space and is the world's biggest single structure made by living organisms. This reef structure is composed of and built by billions of tiny organisms, known as coral polyps. It supports a wide diversity of life and was selected as a World Heritage Site in 1981. CNN labelled it one of the Seven Natural Wonders of the World in 1997. Australian World Heritage places included it in its list in 2007. The Queensland National Trust named it a state icon of Queensland in 2006.

answer: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928[3]. The mass production of penicillin was led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at the Radcliffe Infirmary in Oxford, with support from World War II military projects[1]. By mid-1942, the Oxford team produced the pure penicillin compound as yellow powder[1]. The British War Cabinet set up the Penicillin Committee on 5 April 1943, after clinical trials showed penicillin's effectiveness, and this led to mass production by the next year[4]. The private sector and the United States Department of Agriculture also located and produced new strains and developed mass production techniques[2].

top.text:
As late as in 1939, Fleming's notebook shows attempts to make better penicillin production using different media. In 1941, he published a method for assessment of penicillin effectiveness. As to the chemical isolation and purification, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at the Radcliffe Infirmary in Oxford took up the research to mass-produce it, which they achieved with support from World War II military projects under the British and US governments.
By mid-1942, the Oxford team produced the pure penicillin compound as yellow powder. In August 1942, Harry Lambert (an associate of Fleming's brother Robert) was admitted to St Mary's Hospital due to a life-threatening infection of the nervous system (streptococcal meningitis). Fleming treated him with sulphonamides, but Lambert's condition deteriorated. He tested the antibiotic susceptibility and found that his penicillin could kill the bacteria. At Fleming's request, Florey sent the incompletely purified sample, which Fleming immediately administered into Lambert's spinal canal. Lambert showed signs of improvement the very next day, and completely recovered within a week. Fleming published the clinical case in The Lancet in 1943.

history.answer: Marie Curie (1867–1934) was a Polish and naturalised-French physicist and chemist[1]. She is credited with discovering radioactive polonium and radium, and she remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields[2]. She died in 1934 from aplastic anaemia likely caused by radiation exposure during her scientific work[4]. Her notable work includes a Treatise on Radioactivity[5].

top.text:
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci. Considered an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance, it has been described as "the best known, the most visited, the most written about, the most sung about, [and] the most parodied work of art in the world." The painting's novel qualities include the subject's enigmatic expression, the monumentality of the composition, the subtle modelling of forms, and the atmospheric illusionism.
The painting has been traditionally considered to depict the Italian noblewoman Lisa del Giocondo. It is painted in oil on a white poplar panel. Leonardo never gave the painting to the Giocondo family. It was believed to have been painted between 1503 and 1506; however, Leonardo may have continued working on it as late as 1517. King Francis I of France acquired the Mona Lisa after Leonardo's death in 1519, and it became the property of the French Republic. It has normally been on display at the Louvre in Paris since 1797.

top.text:
The cell cycle, or cell-division cycle, is the sequence of events that take place in a cell and lead to its division into two daughter cells. These events include the growth of the cell, duplication of its DNA (DNA replication) and some of its organelles, and subsequently the partitioning of its cytoplasm, chromosomes and other components into two daughter cells in a process called cell division.
In eukaryotic cells (having a cell nucleus) including animal, plant, fungal, and protist cells, the cell cycle is divided into two main stages: interphase, and the M phase that includes mitosis and cytokinesis. During interphase, the cell grows, accumulating nutrients needed for mitosis, and replicates its DNA and some of its organelles.  Its successive stages differ in their specialized biochemical processes, preparing the cell for initiation of the cell's division, but are not usually morphologically distinguishable.  During the M phase, the replicated chromosomes, organelles, and cytoplasm separate into two new daughter cells. To ensure the proper replication of cellular components and division, cell cycle checkpoints follow each of the key stages of the cycle, controlling whether the cell progresses to the next.

Neil Alden Armstrong (August 5, 1930 – August 25, 2012) was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who, as the commander of the 1969 Apollo 11 mission, became the first person to walk on the Moon. He was also a naval aviator, test pilot and university professor.
Armstrong was born and raised near Wapakoneta, Ohio. He entered Purdue University, studying aeronautical engineering, with the United States Navy paying his tuition under the Holloway Plan.  He became a midshipman in 1949 and a naval aviator the following year. He saw action in the Korean War, flying the Grumman F9F Panther from the aircraft carrier . After the war, he completed his bachelor's degree at Purdue and became a test pilot at the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) High-Speed Flight Station at Edwards Air Force Base in California. He was the project pilot on Century Series fighters and flew the North American X-15 seven times. He was also a participant in the U.S. Air Force's Man in Space Soonest and X-20 Dyna-Soar human spaceflight programs.

history.answer: GPS works by using a network of satellites to determine the location of a receiver on Earth. The Global Positioning System (GPS) is operated by the United States Space Force and provides geolocation and time information[1][5]. A GPS receiver measures the relative time delay of signals from at least four satellites, each of which has atomic clocks that provide very accurate timing[2]. The signals include ranging signals to measure the distance to the satellite and navigation messages, allowing the receiver to calculate its Position, Velocity, and Time (PVT)[3].

answer:
GPS works by using a network of satellites to determine the location of a receiver on Earth. Each GPS satellite carries an accurate record of its own position and time, and broadcasts that data continuously. Based on data received from multiple GPS satellites, an end user's GPS receiver can calculate its own four-dimensional position in spacetime; however, at a minimum, four satellites must be in view of the receiver for it to compute four unknown quantities (three position coordinates and the deviation of its own clock from satellite time)[1].

The receiver's Earth-centered solution location is usually converted to latitude, longitude and height relative to an ellipsoidal Earth model. These coordinates may be displayed, such as on a moving map display, or recorded or used by some other system, such as a vehicle guidance system. As of 2025, these core principles are being enhanced by the ongoing modernization of the GPS constellation with the introduction of GPS III and GPS IIIF satellites[3].

The GPS makes corrections for receiver clock errors and other effects, but there are still residual errors which are not corrected. GPS receiver position is computed based on data received from the satellites. Errors depend on geometric dilution of precision and the sources listed in the table below[2].

top.text:
The GPS satellites carry very stable atomic clocks that are synchronized with one another and with the reference atomic clocks at the ground control stations; any drift of the clocks aboard the satellites from the reference time maintained on the ground stations is corrected regularly. Since the speed of radio waves (speed of light) is constant and independent of the satellite speed, the time delay between when the satellite transmits a signal and the ground station receives it is proportional to the distance from the satellite to the ground station. With the distance information collected from multiple ground stations, the location coordinates of any satellite at any time can be calculated with great precision.

history.answer:
Isaac Newton was an English polymath born in 1643 who was a mathematician, physicist, astronomer, alchemist, theologian, author, and inventor. He was a key figure in the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment, and he made seminal contributions to optics and infinitesimal calculus[1][2].

Newton is best known for his work on the laws of motion and universal gravitation, which he published in his major work, the *Principia Mathematica*[1][4]. He also wrote extensively on theology and alchemy, and he was considered an insightful and erudite theologian by his contemporaries[3]. His religious views were nontrinitarian, and he saw a monotheistic God as the masterful creator of the natural world[3].

Newton was a student of Isaac Barrow and Benjamin Pulleyn, and his notable works include the *Principia Mathematica*, *Method of Fluxions*, *Opticks*, and other treatises on optics and mathematics[5]. He is widely regarded as one of the most influential scientists in human history.

top.text: Sir Isaac Newton (;  – ) was an English polymath who was a mathematician, physicist, astronomer, alchemist, theologian, author and inventor. He was a key figure in the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment that followed. His book Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), first published in 1687, achieved the first great unification in physics and established classical mechanics. Newton also made seminal contributions to optics, and shares credit with the German mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz for formulating infinitesimal calculus, although he developed calculus years before Leibniz. Newton contributed to and refined the scientific method, and his work is considered the most influential in bringing forth modern science.

The comparison is stark: Venus is a scorching, dense, greenhouse world, while Mars is a cold, thin, dry desert.

top.text:
The mean apparent magnitude of Mars is +0.71 with a standard deviation of 1.05. Because the orbit of Mars is eccentric, the magnitude at opposition from the Sun can range from about −3.0 to −1.4. The minimum brightness is magnitude +1.86 when the planet is near aphelion and in conjunction with the Sun. At its brightest, Mars (along with Jupiter) is second only to Venus in apparent brightness. Mars usually appears distinctly yellow, orange, or red. When farthest away from Earth, it is more than seven times farther away than when it is closest. Mars is usually close enough for particularly good viewing once or twice at 15-year or 17-year intervals. Optical ground-based telescopes are typically limited to resolving features about 300 km (190 mi) across when Earth and Mars are closest because of Earth's atmosphere.
As Mars approaches opposition, it begins a period of retrograde motion, which means it will appear to move backwards in a looping curve with respect to the background stars. This retrograde motion lasts for about 72 days, and Mars reaches its peak apparent brightness in the middle of this interval.

K2, also known as Mount Godwin-Austen, at 8611 metres above sea level, is the second-highest mountain on Earth, after Mount Everest at 8849 metres. It lies in the Karakoram range, partially in the Gilgit-Baltistan region of Pakistan-administered Kashmir and partially in the China-administered Trans-Karakoram Tract in the Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County of Xinjiang.
K2 became known as the Savage Mountain after George Bell—a climber on the 1953 American expedition—said, "It's a savage mountain that tries to kill you." Of the five highest mountains in the world, K2 has long been the deadliest: prior to 2021, approximately one person had died on the mountain for every four who reached the summit. After an increase in successful attempts, As of August 2023, an estimated 800 people have summited K2, with 96 deaths during attempted climbs.

answer: Japan has a population of roughly 123.4 million people[1][2], while Germany has a population of 84.7 million according to the 2023 census[1]. Japan is the 6th-most populous country in Asia and the 11th-most populous in the world, whereas Germany is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia[2]. Japan has the second-highest median age in the world, behind only Monaco, and is one of the fastest aging countries, with one-third of its population being elderly[2]. In contrast, Germany has the fourth oldest population in the world, with an average age of 47.8 years[1], and since the 1970s its death rate has exceeded its birth rate[1].

history.answer:
A crocodile is a large, semiaquatic reptile in the family Crocodylidae that lives in tropical regions of Africa, Asia, the Americas, and Australia[1]. It is related to gharials and other extinct taxa[1].

Crocodiles are carnivorous predators that eat fish, amphibians, crustaceans, molluscs, birds, reptiles, and mammals, with diet varying by species, size, and age[3]. They are also farmed commercially for their skin and other products[4]. In politics, the term "crocodile" is used as a nickname or metaphor to describe politicians or groups, often implying qualities like patience, cunning, resilience, or ruthlessness[2].

answer: A crocodile is a large, semiaquatic reptile in the family Crocodylidae, while an alligator belongs to the family Alligatoridae. The most obvious external difference is the shape of the head and snout: crocodiles have narrower, longer heads with a more V-shaped snout, whereas alligators have wider, shovel-like, U-shaped snouts[1][2]. In terms of temperament, crocodiles are generally considered more aggressive than alligators[4].

top.text:
While there are rules of thumb for distinguishing alligators from crocodiles, all of them admit exceptions. Such general rules include:
Exposed vs. interdigitated teeth: The easiest way to distinguish crocodiles from alligators is by looking at their jaw line. The teeth on the lower jaw of an alligator fit into sockets in the upper jaw, leaving only the upper teeth visible when the mouth is closed. The teeth on the lower jaw of a crocodile fit into grooves on the outside of the top jaw, making both the upper and lower teeth visible when the mouth is closed, thus creating a "toothy grin". Shape of the nose and jaw: Alligators have wider, shovel-like, U-shaped snouts, while crocodile snouts are typically more pointed or V-shaped. The alligators' broader snouts have been contentiously thought to allow their jaws to withstand the stress of cracking open the shells of turtles and other hard-shelled animals that are widespread in their environments. A 2012 study found very little correlation between bite force and snout shape amongst 23 tested crocodilian species.

sources.text: A crocodile (family Crocodylidae) or true crocodile is a large, semiaquatic reptile that lives throughout the tropics in Africa, Asia, the Americas and Australia. The term "crocodile" is sometimes used more loosely to include all extant members of the order Crocodilia, which includes the alligators and caimans (both members of the family Alligatoridae), the gharial and false gharial (both members of the family Gavialidae) as well as other extinct taxa.

The gharial, with its narrow snout, is easier to distinguish, while morphological differences are more difficult to spot in crocodiles and alligators. The most obvious external differences are visible in the head, with crocodiles having narrower and longer heads, with a more V-shaped than a U-shaped snout compared to alligators and caimans.

history.answer: Napoleon Bonaparte (born 15 August 1769) was an Emperor of the French from 1804 until his first abdication in 1814. He rose to prominence as a general during the French Revolution, leading military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East during the Napoleonic Wars[1][2]. As First Consul from 1799, he later became Emperor of the French Empire[3]. His legacy is highly polarized: he is typically loved or hated, with few nuances, and his name is associated with tactical brilliance, ambition, and political power[4][5].

answer: Napoleon and Alexander the Great were both brilliant military commanders who built large empires, but their careers differed in scope and duration. Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire and by age 30 had created one of the largest empires in history, stretching from Greece to northwestern India[1][4]. Napoleon led a series of military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, building a vast empire that lasted until his first abdication in 1814[2]. While both were tactical geniuses, Alexander’s campaign was more concentrated and shorter, whereas Napoleon’s wars spanned decades and involved many more nations.

top.text: Alexander III of Macedon (; 20/21 July 356 BC – 10/11 June 323 BC), most commonly known as Alexander the Great, was king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon from 336 BC until his death. He was the son of Philip II, born to him by his fourth wife, Olympias, and ascended to the throne at the age of 20 after Philip was assassinated. Alexander spent most of his reign conducting a lengthy military campaign throughout Asia and Egypt, and by the age of 30, he had created one of the largest empires in history, stretching from Greece to northwestern India. He was undefeated in battle and is widely considered to be one of history's greatest and most successful military commanders.

answer:
The Amazon River is generally considered the second longest river in the world, with the Nile being the longest[3]. However, there is ongoing debate about which is truly the longest. The Amazon's length is reported as anywhere between 6,275 km and 6,992 km[3], while a 2009 peer-reviewed study found the Nile to be 7,088 km long and the Amazon 6,575 km[4]. The Nile is 6,650 km long according to Wikidata[1].

The Amazon River flows through South America, with its headwaters in the Andes of Peru and its mouth in Brazil, while the Nile flows through northeastern Africa[2].

sources.text: The Nile has two major tributaries: the White Nile and the Blue Nile. The White Nile is longer and is considered to be the headwaters, yet the Blue Nile contributes over twice the water volume of the White Nile. The White Nile begins near Lake Victoria and flows through Uganda and South Sudan, while the Blue Nile begins near Lake Tana in Ethiopia and flows into Sudan from the southeast. The two rivers meet at the Sudanese capital, Khartoum.

history.answer: Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language known for its emphasis on code readability, simplicity, and ease of writing. It supports multiple programming paradigms—object-oriented programming, structured programming, functional programming, and metaprogramming—and features an extensive standard library, dynamic typing, and automatic memory management. Python was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991[1][2][4].

answer: Python differs from Java in several key ways. First, Python is dynamically typed and uses automatic memory management, whereas Java is statically typed and requires manual memory management[4][5]. Second, Python emphasizes code readability and simplicity with significant indentation, while Java prioritizes performance and safety[1][4]. Third, Python supports multiple programming paradigms—object-oriented, structured, functional, and metaprogramming—while Java is primarily object-oriented[1][3]. Fourth, Python has a large standard library that is "batteries-included," whereas Java's ecosystem is more fragmented across platforms[4]. Finally, Python can be used as a scripting language or for hardware description (MyHDL), and Jython allows Python 2.7 to run on the JVM, but Java is a standalone, compiled language designed for cross-platform execution[1][2].

top.text: Java is a high-level, general-purpose, memory-safe, object-oriented programming language. It is intended to let programmers write once, run anywhere (WORA), meaning that compiled Java code can run on all platforms that support Java without the need to recompile. Java applications are usually compiled to bytecode that can run on any Java virtual machine (JVM) regardless of the underlying computer architecture. The syntax of Java is similar to C and C++, but has fewer low-level facilities than either of them. The Java runtime provides dynamic abilities (such as reflective programming (reflection) and runtime code modification) usually unavailable in traditional compiled languages.

history.answer: The sky looks blue because of Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight contains all visible colours, and when it passes through the atmosphere it hits nitrogen and oxygen molecules that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. These molecules scatter short wavelengths far more strongly than long ones: scattering grows with the inverse fourth power of the wavelength, so blue light at about 450 nm is scattered almost six times more than red light at 700 nm. The scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every direction, so the whole sky looks blue. Violet light is scattered even more, but the Sun emits less of it, some is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunrise and sunset, light travels through much more air, most of the blue is scattered away before it reaches us, and the sky near the Sun turns orange and red.

answer: The sky is blue because of Rayleigh scattering: sunlight hits nitrogen and oxygen molecules, which scatter short wavelengths like blue light far more strongly than long ones. The scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every direction, making the whole sky look blue.

history.answer: A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise a germ without causing the disease. It contains a harmless form or part of the pathogen: a killed or weakened virus, a purified protein, or genetic instructions such as mRNA that make the body's own cells produce one viral protein. The immune system treats this antigen as a threat. B cells make antibodies that bind to it, and T cells learn to recognise and kill infected cells. Some of these cells become long-lived memory cells. If the real pathogen later enters the body, the memory cells recognise it and mount a fast, strong response, often before the person gets sick. Some vaccines need booster doses to keep immunity high. When enough people in a population are immune, the germ spreads less, which also protects people who cannot be vaccinated; this is called herd immunity.

answer: A vaccine is like a practice lesson for your body's defense system. It gives your immune system a harmless copy of a germ, like a killed virus or a piece of its protein. Your body then makes antibodies to fight it and remembers how to do so. If you ever meet the real germ later, your body can spot it and attack it quickly, often before you get sick. Some vaccines need extra doses (booster shots) to keep this protection strong. When enough people in a community are vaccinated, the germ can't spread as easily, which protects everyone, including those who can't get the vaccine.

history.answer: World War I had long-term causes and a short-term trigger. The trigger was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary by the Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, sent an ultimatum to Serbia and declared war on 28 July. The alliance system then pulled in the other powers: Russia mobilised to support Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and Britain entered after Germany invaded neutral Belgium. Behind this lay deeper causes: nationalism in the Balkans and across Europe, rivalry between empires over colonies and trade, an arms race that included the Anglo-German naval race, and military plans such as Germany's Schlieffen Plan that made fast mobilisation and war more likely once a crisis began.

- Britain entered the war after Germany invaded neutral Belgium.

history.answer: Inflation is the general rise in the prices of goods and services over time, which means each unit of money buys less. It is usually measured as the yearly percentage change in a price index such as the consumer price index (CPI), which tracks the cost of a typical basket of goods. Inflation can come from strong demand that outpaces supply (demand-pull), from rising production costs such as energy or wages (cost-push), or from fast growth of the money supply. Most central banks aim for low and stable inflation, often around 2 percent a year, and raise interest rates to slow it. Very high inflation, called hyperinflation, destroys savings, as in Germany in 1923 or Zimbabwe in the late 2000s. The opposite, a general fall in prices, is deflation.

answer: Inflation is the general rise in prices over time, driven by factors like strong demand or rising costs, and is measured as a yearly percentage change in a price index. Central banks aim for low, stable inflation, while hyperinflation can destroy savings.

history.answer: Most black holes form when a very massive star dies. A star is held up against its own gravity by the pressure from nuclear fusion in its core. When a star of more than about 20 solar masses runs out of fuel, fusion stops and the core collapses in a fraction of a second. The outer layers may be blown off in a supernova explosion. If the remaining core is more than about three solar masses, no known force can stop the collapse, and it shrinks until its gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from inside a boundary called the event horizon. Black holes then grow by pulling in gas and by merging with other black holes. The supermassive black holes at the centres of galaxies, with millions to billions of solar masses, grew this way, though how they formed so early in the universe is still an open question.

answer: Black holes form when very massive stars collapse under their own gravity. This collapse can happen directly or during a supernova explosion[3][4]. The star's core runs out of fuel, so it can no longer support itself against gravity, and the star collapses into a black hole[3].

history.query: What is the theory of evolution?
history.answer: The theory of evolution explains how living things change over generations and how all species descend from common ancestors. Its main mechanism, natural selection, was described by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in 1858, and Darwin set it out in On the Origin of Species (1859). Individuals in a population vary, much of this variation is inherited, and more offspring are born than can survive. Those with traits that suit their environment tend to survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over time. Genetics later explained the source of the variation: mutations and the recombination of genes. Other forces, such as genetic drift and gene flow, also change populations. Over long periods these changes can produce new species. The evidence comes from fossils, comparative anatomy, the geographic spread of species and DNA.

answer: The theory of evolution is the explanation for how living things change over generations and how all species descend from common ancestors, with natural selection as its main mechanism[2][3]. It was independently described by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in the mid-19th century, and Darwin set it out in detail in *On the Origin of Species* (1859)[2][3]. The theory is a well-substantiated explanation of facts, including observational evidence of current processes and transitions in the fossil record[5].

top.text:
Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (; 10 December 1815 – 27 November 1852), also known as Ada Lovelace, was an English mathematician and writer chiefly known for work on Charles Babbage's proposed mechanical general-purpose computer, the analytical engine. She was the first to recognise the machine had applications beyond pure calculation. Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
Lovelace was the only legitimate child of poet Lord Byron and reformer Anne Isabella Milbanke. Lord Byron separated from his wife a month after Ada was born, and died when she was eight. Although often ill in childhood, Lovelace pursued her studies assiduously. She married William King in 1835. King was a Baron, and was created Viscount Ockham and 1st Earl of Lovelace in 1838. The name Lovelace was chosen because Ada was descended from the extinct Baron Lovelaces. The title given to her husband thus made Ada the Countess of Lovelace.

history.query: What is the Great Wall of China?
history.answer: The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across China's northern borders to aid in defense[1]. It includes watchtowers, troop barracks, garrison stations, and signaling capabilities, and it also served as a border control system to regulate immigration, emigration, and trade along the Silk Road[1]. The most visible parts today are from the Ming dynasty (1368–1644)[2], though the wall's history stretches back to the 7th century, with the oldest existing section built by the Qi state in 441 BC[5]. The full extent of the wall is difficult to define because no single formal definition has been agreed upon, and the remaining associated sites are estimated at over 10,000 kilometers[4].

top.text:
The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications in China. They were built across the historical northern borders of ancient Chinese states and Imperial China as protection against various nomadic groups from the Eurasian Steppe. The first walls date to the 7th century BC; these were joined together in the Qin dynasty. Successive dynasties expanded the wall system; the best-known sections were built by the Ming dynasty (1368–1644).
To aid in defense, the Great Wall utilized watchtowers, troop barracks, garrison stations, signaling capabilities through the means of smoke or fire, and its status as a transportation corridor. Other purposes of the Great Wall have included border controls (allowing control of immigration and emigration, and the imposition of duties on goods transported along the Silk Road), and the regulation of trade.

answer: Hamlet is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare sometime between 1599 and 1601[1][2]. It tells the story of Prince Hamlet, who seeks revenge against his uncle Claudius for murdering his father and marrying his mother[1]. The play charts Hamlet's real or feigned madness as he grapples with grief, betrayal, and moral conflict[1]. It is Shakespeare's longest play and is widely considered one of the greatest works of literature[1][2].

history.query: What is the Hubble Space Telescope?
history.answer: The Hubble Space Telescope (HST) is a space telescope launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and still in operation[1][2]. It is named after astronomer Edwin Hubble and is one of NASA's Great Observatories program[1][4]. Hubble features a 2.4 m mirror and observes in the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared regions[3]. Its orbit outside Earth's atmosphere allows it to capture extremely high-resolution images with lower background light than ground-based telescopes[3]. The Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI) selects its targets and processes data, while the Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) controls the spacecraft[1].

answer:
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 because it is a space telescope designed to observe from outside Earth's atmosphere[1][2]. Building it on the ground would have been limited by atmospheric interference and the need for a large, complex structure that could not be constructed without the advantages of space-based observation.

The Hubble Space Telescope was funded and built in the 1970s by NASA with contributions from the European Space Agency, but its launch was delayed due to technical problems, budget issues, and the Challenger disaster[2]. The Great Observatories program, which includes Hubble, was launched between 1990 and 2003 to provide powerful astrophysical tools that cannot be achieved from the ground[3][4]. By being in space, Hubble can capture extremely high-resolution images with lower background light than ground-based telescopes[1].

Its intended launch was in 1983, but the project was beset by technical delays, budget problems, and the 1986 Challenger disaster. Hubble was launched on STS-31 in 1990, but its main mirror had been ground incorrectly, resulting in spherical aberration that compromised the telescope's capabilities.

history.answer:
Genghis Khan, born Temüjin around 1162, was the founder and first khan of the Mongol Empire[1]. He spent most of his life uniting the Mongol tribes and then launched a series of military campaigns that conquered large parts of China and Central Asia[1][2].

He was both generous and intensely loyal to his followers, but ruthless towards his enemies. He welcomed advice from diverse sources in his quest for world domination, believing the shamanic supreme deity Tengri had destined him[2]. The Mongol army under Genghis Khan killed millions of people, yet his conquests also facilitated unprecedented commercial and cultural exchange over a vast geographical area[2].

Temüjin formally adopted the title "Genghis Khan" at an assembly in 1206, after thwarting a coup attempt from a powerful shaman and consolidating his power[3]. The following year, he invaded the Khwarazmian Empire after the execution of his envoys, which toppled that state and devastated regions of Transoxiana and Khorasan[3].

His legacy has inspired numerous works of literature, films, and other media, and many products and places are named after him[4].

answer: The capital of Japan is Tokyo, but the country has had many capitals throughout history[1][2]. The oldest was Nara, and the most famous was Heian-kyō (modern Kyoto), which served as the capital from 794 to 1868[4][5]. Before that, the capital moved around among several sites, including Ōtsu and Nagaoka-kyō[2]. The current capital, Tokyo, became the seat of government in 1868 when the Emperor moved there from Edo[1].

top.text:
Traditionally, the home of the Emperor is considered the capital. From 794 through 1868, the Emperor lived in Heian-kyō, modern-day Kyoto. After 1868, the seat of the Government of Japan and the location of the Emperor's home was moved to Edo, which it renamed Tokyo. This term for capital was never used to refer to Kyoto. Indeed, shuto came into use during the 1860s as a gloss of the English term "capital".
In 1941, the Ministry of Education published the "designation of Tokyo as capital" (東京奠都). The Ministry of Education published a book called "History of the Restoration" in 1941. This book referred to "designating Tokyo as capital" (東京奠都) without talking about "relocating the capital to Tokyo" (東京遷都). A contemporary history textbook states that the Meiji government "moved the capital (shuto) from Kyoto to Tokyo" without using the sento term.

answer: If the pancreas stops making insulin, the body can no longer regulate blood sugar effectively. Without insulin, glucose remains in the bloodstream instead of being taken up by cells, leading to high blood sugar levels (hyperglycaemia)[1]. This is the core problem in type 1 diabetes, where the beta cells that produce insulin are destroyed by an autoimmune reaction[1]. In type 2 diabetes, the body still makes insulin but the cells do not respond to it properly, a condition called insulin resistance[4]. The pancreas normally releases insulin in short bursts after meals, and without this regulation, blood sugar levels would remain elevated[3].

top.text: Decreased or absent insulin activity results in diabetes, a condition of high blood sugar level (hyperglycaemia). There are two types of the disease. In type 1 diabetes, the beta cells are destroyed by an autoimmune reaction so that insulin can no longer be synthesized or be secreted into the blood. In type 2 diabetes, the destruction of beta cells is less pronounced than in type 1, and is not due to an autoimmune process. Instead, there is an accumulation of amyloid in the pancreatic islets, which likely disrupts their anatomy and physiology. The pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes is not well understood but reduced population of islet beta-cells, reduced secretory function of islet beta-cells that survive, and peripheral tissue insulin resistance are known to be involved. Type 2 diabetes is characterized by increased glucagon secretion which is unaffected by, and unresponsive to the concentration of blood glucose. However, insulin is still secreted into the blood in response to the blood glucose. As a result, glucose accumulates in the blood.

sources.text: The liver clears most insulin during first-pass transit, whereas the kidney clears most of the insulin in systemic circulation.  Degradation normally involves endocytosis of the insulin-receptor complex, then the action of insulin-degrading … An insulin molecule produced endogenously by the beta cells is estimated to be degraded within about one hour after its initial release into circulation (insulin half-life ~ 4–6 minutes).

sources.text: Even during digestion, in general, one or two hours following a meal, insulin release from the pancreas is not continuous, but oscillates with a period of 3–6 minutes, changing from generating a blood insulin concentration more than about 800 p mol/l to less than 100 pmol/L (in rats). This is thought to avoid downregulation of insulin receptors in target cells, and to assist the liver in extracting insulin from the blood.

sources.title: Insulin resistance
sources.text: At the molecular level, a cell senses insulin through insulin receptors, with the signal propagating through the insulin signal transduction pathway. Recent studies suggested that the pathway may operate as a bistable switch under physiologic conditions for certain types of cells, and insulin response may well be a threshold phenomenon. The pathway's sensitivity to insulin may be blunted by many factors such as lipolysis of free fatty acids, causing insulin resistance.

answer: The Eiffel Tower was designed by engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, with architectural contributions from Stephen Sauvestre[1][2]. It was not meant to be permanent; the tower was built as a temporary exhibit for the 1889 Universal Exposition and was originally scheduled to be dismantled after 20 years[1][4]. However, Gustave Eiffel recognized its scientific value—particularly its use in meteorology and radio transmission—and successfully lobbied for its preservation, so it has remained standing ever since[1].

top.text: The design of the Eiffel Tower is attributed to Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, two senior engineers working for the Compagnie des Établissements Eiffel. It was envisaged after discussion about a suitable centrepiece for the proposed 1889 Exposition Universelle, a world's fair to celebrate the centennial of the French Revolution. In May 1884, working at home, Koechlin made a sketch of their idea, described by him as "a great pylon, consisting of four lattice girders standing apart at the base and coming together at the top, joined together by metal trusses at regular intervals". Eiffel initially showed little enthusiasm, but he did approve further study, and the two engineers then asked Stephen Sauvestre, the head of the company's architectural department, to contribute to the design. Sauvestre added decorative arches to the base of the tower, a glass pavilion to the first level, and other embellishments.

history.answer: Volcanoes form in several different settings. In subduction zones, hydrous minerals on a descending plate release water into the mantle, which lowers the melting point and causes magma to form[4]. At mid-ocean ridges or hotspots, tectonic stretching thins the crust and allows hot mantle material to rise, producing volcanic island chains like Hawaii[1][2]. When magma reaches the surface through a convergent boundary or a hotspot, it builds a volcano such as a shield or stratovolcano[2]. The magma itself is made of volatile rock dissolved in molten rock, and the eruptions produce lava, ash, tephra, and volcanic rock[5].

answer: Volcanoes form in several different settings. In subduction zones, hydrous minerals on a descending plate release water into the mantle, which lowers the melting point and causes magma to form[1]. Shield volcanoes are formed by low-viscosity basaltic or andesitic lava that flows far from a vent, and they are more common in oceanic settings than continental ones; Olympus Mons on Mars is an extinct shield volcano[2]. Hotspots are created by mantle plumes, columns of hot material rising from the core-mantle boundary; decompression melting generates magma, and as plates move over the plume, new volcanoes form while older ones become inactive[3]. Most volcanic activity occurs along plate boundaries where lithosphere is being destroyed or formed, and some volcanoes are polygenetic with multiple periods of activity[4].

top.text: Shield volcanoes, so named for their broad, shield-like profiles, are formed by the eruption of low-viscosity basaltic or andesitic lava that can flow a great distance from a vent. They generally do not explode catastrophically but are characterized by relatively gentle effusive eruptions. Since low-viscosity magma is typically low in silica, shield volcanoes are more common in oceanic than continental settings. The Hawaiian volcanic chain is a series of shield cones, and they are common in Iceland, as well. Olympus Mons, an extinct martian shield volcano is the largest known volcano in the Solar System.

It was drafted by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Cardinal Stephen Langton, to make peace between the unpopular king and rebel barons who demanded that the King confirm the Charter of Liberties[1]. answer:
The Magna Carta is a royal charter of rights sealed by King John of England at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215[5]. It was drafted by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Cardinal Stephen Langton, to make peace between the unpopular king and rebel barons who demanded that the King confirm the Charter of Liberties[1]. The document established the principle that everyone, including the king, was subject to the law, and it has since become a foundational symbol for constitutional rights and the rule of law[2][4].

The 800th anniversary in 2015 included extensive celebrations and discussions, and the four original 1215 charters were displayed together at the British Library[2]. None of the original 1215 Magna Carta is currently in force since it has been repealed; however, three clauses of the original charter are enshrined in the 1297 reissued Magna Carta and do still remain in force in England and Wales[2]. The legal profession in England and the United States continued to hold Magna Carta in high esteem; they were instrumental in forming the Magna Carta Society in 1922 to protect the meadows at Runnymede from development[1].

The charter's influence extends beyond England. For example, Hugh of Wells, Bishop of Lincoln, was one of the signatories to Magna Carta and for hundreds of years the cathedral held one of the four remaining copies of the original, now securely displayed in Lincoln Castle[3]. The Lincoln Magna Carta was on display at the British Pavilion during the 1939 New York World's Fair and was lent to the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, California in 2009[3].

top.text:
This view also became popular in wider circles, and in 1930 Sellar and Yeatman published their parody on English history, 1066 and All That, in which they mocked the supposed importance of Magna Carta and its promises of universal liberty: "Magna Charter was therefore the chief cause of Democracy in England, and thus a Good Thing for everyone (except the Common People)".
In many literary representations of the medieval past, however, Magna Carta remained a foundation of English national identity. Some authors used the medieval roots of the document as an argument to preserve the social status quo, while others pointed to Magna Carta to challenge perceived economic injustices. The Baronial Order of Magna Charta was formed in 1898 to promote the ancient principles and values felt to be displayed in Magna Carta. The legal profession in England and the United States continued to hold Magna Carta in high esteem; they were instrumental in forming the Magna Carta Society in 1922 to protect the meadows at Runnymede from development in the 1920s, and in 1957, the American Bar Association erected the Magna Carta Memorial at Runnymede. The prominent lawyer Lord Denning described Magna Carta in 1956 as "the greatest constitutional document of all times—the foundation of the freedom of the individual against the arbitrary authority of the despot".

The heart is connected to the entire body through the circulation, and its function is regulated by the brainstem’s cardiovascular centres via the vagus nerve and sympathetic trunk[4].

answer:
The heart works by pumping blood throughout the body, with an electrical conduction system that controls contraction and relaxation. The sinoatrial node generates action potentials that spread to nearby cardiomyocytes, creating the normal sinus rhythm[1]. When these contractions occur in a coordinated fashion, the atria and ventricles pump, delivering blood to the rest of the body[2].

The heart has two atria and two ventricles that work in concert. At the start of the cycle, during ventricular diastole, the heart relaxes and expands while receiving blood into both ventricles through both atria; then, near the end of ventricular diastole, the two atria begin to contract[5]. The heart tissue is supplied by two arteries arising just above the aortic valve: the left anterior descending artery supplies the front, outer side, and septum of the left ventricle, while the right coronary artery runs in a groove at the back of the heart[4].

These impulses ultimately stimulate heart muscle to contract and thereby to eject blood from the ventricles into the arteries and the cardiac circulatory system; and they provide a system of intricately timed and persistent signaling that controls the rhythmic beating of the heart muscle cells, especially the complex impulse-generation and muscle contractions in the atrial chambers.

record.search_query: How does the heart work?

segments.Text: The heart works by pumping blood throughout the body, with an electrical conduction system that controls contraction and relaxation. The sinoatrial node generates action potentials that spread to nearby cardiomyocytes, creating the normal sinus rhythm
. When these contractions occur in a coordinated fashion, the atria and ventricles pump, delivering blood to the rest of the body

.

The heart has two atria and two ventricles that work in concert. At the start of the cycle, during ventricular diastole, the heart relaxes and expands while receiving blood into both ventricles through both atria; then, near the end of ventricular diastole, the two atria begin to contract

. The heart tissue is supplied by two arteries arising just above the aortic valve: the left anterior descending artery supplies the front, outer side, and septum of the left ventricle, while the right coronary artery runs in a groove at the back of the heart

history.answer: Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence that involves constructing and studying systems that can learn from data[1][2]. It is a scientific discipline that deals with the construction and study of algorithms that can learn from data, and it is used in computing tasks where designing explicit, rule-based algorithms is infeasible[3]. Machine learning has evolved from pattern recognition and computational learning theory, and it encompasses approaches such as supervised learning, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and self-supervised learning[5]. Most traditional machine learning and deep learning algorithms can be described as empirical risk minimisation under a theoretical framework[2].

answer:
Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence and a scientific discipline focused on constructing systems that can learn from data[1]. It involves algorithms that improve their performance on a given task automatically, without being explicitly programmed[1].

There are several types of machine learning. Unsupervised learning analyzes a stream of data, finds patterns, and makes predictions without any other guidance[1]. Supervised learning builds a mathematical model of a set of data containing both inputs and desired outputs, then uses iterative optimization to learn a function that can predict outputs for new inputs[2]. Reinforcement learning is concerned with how software agents should take actions in an environment to maximize cumulative reward, typically represented as a Markov decision process[3].

Machine learning models are statistical and probabilistic models that capture patterns in data through computational algorithms[4]. A learning curve shows how a model's performance changes with the number of training iterations or the amount of training data[5]. Machine learning is part of mathematics and artificial intelligence, and it follows pattern recognition and computational learning theory[6].

top.text: Supervised learning algorithms build a mathematical model of a set of data that contains both the inputs and the desired outputs. The data, known as training data, consists of a set of training examples. Each training example has one or more inputs and the desired output, also known as a supervisory signal. In the mathematical model, each training example is represented by an array or vector, sometimes called a feature vector, and the training data is represented by a matrix. Through iterative optimisation of an objective function, supervised learning algorithms learn a function that can be used to predict the output associated with new inputs. An optimal function allows the algorithm to correctly determine the output for inputs that were not a part of the training data. An algorithm that improves the accuracy of its outputs or predictions over time is said to have learned to perform that task.

history.answer: The Renaissance was a cultural and intellectual movement that began in Europe at the end of the Late Middle Ages and the early modern era, centered first in Florence, Italy. It marked a profound change in European intellectual life, characterized by a renewed interest in classical antiquity, humanist methods of study, and a focus on realism and human emotion in art and literature. The movement spread across Italy and then throughout Europe between the 14th and 16th centuries, influencing art, architecture, politics, literature, exploration, and technology. It was supported by royalty, nobility, the Catholic Church, and an emerging merchant class.

answer: The Renaissance was a cultural and intellectual movement that began in Europe at the end of the Late Middle Ages and the early modern era, centered first in Florence, Italy. It marked a profound change in European intellectual life, characterized by a renewed interest in classical antiquity, humanist methods of study, and a focus on realism and human emotion in art and literature[1][2]. The period is often dated from the 14th century to the 17th century, with some historians arguing it started around 1300 and lasted until about 1600[2][3]. The word "renaissance" means "rebirth," reflecting a cultural revival and renewed interest in classical antiquity after centuries of medieval thought[2].

The beginnings of the period—the early Renaissance of the 15th century and the Italian Proto-Renaissance from around 1250 or 1300—overlap considerably with the Late Middle Ages, conventionally dated to c. 1350–1500, and the Middle Ages themselves were a long period filled with gradual changes, like the modern age; as a transitional period between both, the Renaissance has close similarities to both, especially the late and early sub-periods of either.
The Renaissance began in Florence, one of the many states of Italy. The Italian Renaissance concluded in 1527 when Holy Roman Emperor Charles V launched an assault on Rome during the war of the League of Cognac. Nevertheless, its impact endured in the art of renowned Italian painters like Tintoretto, Sofonisba Anguissola, and Paolo Veronese, who continued their work during the mid-to-late 16th century.

top.text: Brazil, officially the Federative Republic of Brazil, is the largest country in South America. It is also the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh-largest by population, with over 214 million people. Brazil is a federation composed of 26 states and a Federal District, which hosts the capital, Brasília. Its most populous city is São Paulo, followed by Rio de Janeiro. Brazil has the largest Lusophone population in the world and is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas, where it is the official language.

The Parthenon (;  ;  ) is a former temple on the Athenian Acropolis, Greece, that was dedicated to the goddess Athena. Its decorative sculptures are considered some of the high points of classical Greek art, and the Parthenon is considered an enduring symbol of ancient Greece, Western civilisation, and democracy.
The Parthenon was built in the 5th century BC in thanksgiving for the Greek victory over the Persian invaders during the Greco-Persian Wars. Like most Greek temples, the Parthenon also served as the city treasury. Construction started in 447 BC when the Delian League was at the peak of its power. It was completed in 438 BC; work on the artwork and decorations continued until 432 BC. For a time, it served as the treasury of the Delian League, which later became the Athenian Empire.

history.answer: A leopard is a large, carnivorous feline in the genus Panthera, with a pale yellowish to dark golden fur marked by dark spots grouped in rosettes[1][2]. It has a slender, muscular body, a long tail, and a shoulder height of 60 to 70 cm[1]. Leopards are found across Africa and Asia, inhabiting tropical forests, plains, deserts, and mountains, and are listed as vulnerable by the IUCN[3]. They have cultural significance in ancient Greece, West Africa, and modern Western culture[2].

answer: The leopard and cheetah are closely related, both in the genus *Panthera*, but they can be told apart by several physical and behavioral differences. The cheetah is smaller and more slender, with a distinctive small, rounded tail and a spotted coat that often has solid spots rather than the rosettes of leopards[1]. The leopard has a stockier build, a long tail, and its fur is marked by dark spots grouped in rosettes[3]. The cheetah’s coat is typically solid-colored spots without the dark ringed patterns of the leopard[1]. In terms of genetics, the two species have been confused historically, but their physical traits remain distinct[1]. A king cheetah, a rare mutation, has large blotchy spots and three stripes down its tail, which can further distinguish it from a typical leopard[4]. The leopard is also more adaptable to various habitats, including forests, mountains, and deserts, while the cheetah is primarily found in open plains[5].

query: How is it different from Hinduism?

history.answer:
Buddhism is a religion and practical philosophy based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, who lived in India in the 5th century BCE[1][2]. It is the world's fourth-largest religion, with about 320 million followers, and is classified as an Indian religion[1][4].

Buddhism does not include belief in a monotheistic creator deity. Instead, it teaches that there are divine beings called devas, but these are not creators or eternal beings[3]. The main focus of Buddhism is on understanding the nature of reality and achieving liberation from the cycle of rebirth (samsara)[1][2].

Buddhism has had a significant role in Asian culture and spirituality, and it spread to the West in the 20th century[1]. It hybridized with Taoism in China by the 4th century AD[2].

answer: Buddhism and Hinduism differ in several key ways. First, Buddhism has a single historical founder, Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, while Hinduism has no single founder and grew out of centuries of interaction between diverse Indian religious groups[4][5]. Second, Hinduism is an umbrella term for a range of traditions unified by adherence to Dharma, a cosmic order maintained through rituals and righteous living, and is classified as an Indian religion[1]. Buddhism, by contrast, is a distinct religion with its own teachings and practices, and it spread throughout Asia via proselytism and conversion[2][3].

history.query: How fast can a cheetah run?
history.answer: A cheetah can reach speeds of up to 114 km/h (71 mph), though this figure has been discredited due to faulty measurement methods[1]. A more reliable record is 98 km/h (61 mph) set by an 11-year-old cheetah at the Cincinnati Zoo[1]. During hunts, GPS collars recorded average speeds of 54 km/h (34 mph) and maximum speeds of 93 km/h (58 mph)[2]. The cheetah’s stride length is 4 to 7 m, and it can take 4 strides per second at full speed[3].

top.text:
The Greyhound is a breed of dog and a sighthound. It is an ancient breed historically developed for hunting game by sight and speed, and has later been used in organised coursing and greyhound racing. Greyhounds are also kept as show dogs and companion animals.
Greyhounds are characterised by a tall, muscular, smooth-coated build, a long tail, tough feet, and a distinctive flexible, "S-shaped" outline typical of sighthounds. They are a distinct breed from other related sighthounds, such as the Italian Greyhound.
The Greyhound's long legs, deep chest, flexible spine, and slim build enable high sprinting speeds. In racing contexts, Greyhounds can reach peak speeds of at least 69 km/h (43 mph), with typical winning speeds of approximately 58-61 km/h.

history.answer: Mercury is the first planet from the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System. It is a rocky planet with a trace atmosphere and a surface gravity slightly lower than that of Mars[1]. The planet is named after the ancient Roman god Mercurius, who was the god of commerce and communication and the messenger of the gods[4]. Mercury is also the name of a chemical element (symbol Hg, atomic number 80) commonly known as quicksilver[2].

answer: Venus is significantly hotter than Mercury. Venus's surface temperature reaches around 464 °C (740 K) due to its dense CO₂ atmosphere and strong greenhouse effect[1][4], while Mercury's surface temperature during sunlight is only about 790 °F (420 K), and its average temperature is around 100 K[2][6]. Venus receives only about 25% of the solar energy per unit area that Mercury does, yet its atmosphere traps far more heat[1].

top.text: Venus has a dense atmosphere composed of 96.5% carbon dioxide, 3.5% nitrogen—both exist as supercritical fluids at the planet's surface with a density 6.5% that of water—and traces of other gases including sulphur dioxide. The mass of its atmosphere is 92 times that of Earth's, whereas the pressure at its surface is about 93 times that at Earth's—a pressure equivalent to that at a depth of nearly 1 km (1 mi) under Earth's ocean surfaces. The density at the surface is 65 kg/m3, 6.5% that of water or 50 times as dense as Earth's atmosphere at 20 °C at sea level. The -rich atmosphere generates the strongest greenhouse effect in the Solar System, creating surface temperatures of at least 462 °C. This makes the Venusian surface hotter than Mercury's, even though Venus is nearly twice Mercury's distance from the Sun and thus receives only around a quarter of Mercury's solar irradiance, of 2,600 W/m2 (double that of Earth). Because of its runaway greenhouse effect, Venus has been identified by scientists such as Carl Sagan as a warning and research object linked to climate change on Earth. Venus has thus been called a greenhouse planet.

history.answer: A refrigerator moves heat from inside the cabinet to the room using a vapor-compression cycle. A refrigerant circulates through a closed loop. The compressor squeezes the refrigerant gas, which raises its pressure and temperature. The hot gas flows through the condenser coils on the back or bottom, where it gives off heat to the room and condenses into a liquid. The liquid then passes through an expansion valve, where its pressure drops suddenly and it becomes very cold. In the evaporator coils inside the fridge, the cold refrigerant absorbs heat from the food compartment and evaporates back into a gas. The gas returns to the compressor and the cycle repeats. A thermostat switches the compressor on and off to hold the set temperature.

history.answer: A stock market is a place where people buy and sell shares of companies. A share, or stock, is a small piece of ownership in a company. Companies sell shares to raise money to grow, and investors buy them hoping the company will do well. Once shares are issued, investors trade them with each other on exchanges such as the New York Stock Exchange or the London Stock Exchange. The price of a share changes with supply and demand: if more people want to buy than sell, the price rises. Investors can earn money when the share price goes up or when the company pays part of its profits as dividends. Stock indexes such as the S&P 500 track the prices of groups of large companies to show how the market as a whole is doing.

You can also earn money from dividends, which is a share of the company's profits. Stock indexes, like the S&P 500, track big companies to show how the whole market is doing.

history.query: What were the causes of the Great Depression?
history.answer: The Great Depression, which began in 1929 and lasted through most of the 1930s, had several connected causes. The stock market crash of October 1929 wiped out wealth and confidence in the United States. Thousands of banks then failed, and because deposits were not insured, savers lost their money and lending dried up. Spending fell, factories cut production and unemployment in the United States rose to about 25 percent by 1933. The gold standard spread the crisis between countries and kept central banks from expanding the money supply. The Smoot–Hawley Tariff of 1930 and tariffs in response abroad shrank world trade. Many economists also blame the Federal Reserve for letting the money supply shrink by about a third.

answer: The Great Depression had several interconnected causes, though they are debated among historians. The main trigger was the Wall Street crash of October 1929, which wiped out wealth and confidence[1][3]. Monetarist economists Milton Friedman and Anna J. Schwartz argued that the banking crisis caused one-third of all banks to fail, a reduction in bank shareholder wealth, and a monetary contraction of 35%, which they called "The Great Contraction"[4]. Marxist theorists generally argue that the Depression was the result of the inherent instability of the capitalist mode of production[5]. Other historians focus on non-monetary causes, with some viewing the crash itself as the main cause and others seeing it as a symptom of deeper economic trends already underway in the late 1920s[2]. The nadir of the Depression came in 1931–1933, with high unemployment, famine, poverty, deflation, and lost opportunities for economic growth[3].

history.answer: Climate change is the long-term change in Earth's climate, and today it mostly refers to the global warming caused by human activity since the Industrial Revolution. Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, and farming and deforestation add more greenhouse gases such as methane. These gases trap heat in the atmosphere, so average global temperatures have risen by about 1.2 °C since the late 19th century. The effects include more frequent heat waves, melting glaciers and ice sheets, rising sea levels, shifting rainfall and more acidic oceans. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, most countries agreed to limit warming to well below 2 °C. Ways to reduce it include switching to renewable energy, using energy more efficiently and protecting forests.

answer: Climate change is the long-term shift in Earth's climate, mainly driven by human activities since the Industrial Revolution, which release greenhouse gases that trap heat and raise average global temperatures by about 1.2 °C, causing more frequent heat waves, melting ice, rising seas, and more acidic oceans.

history.answer: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing. They work by attacking structures or processes that bacteria have but human cells do not. Penicillins and cephalosporins, for example, block the enzymes that build the bacterial cell wall, so the bacteria burst. Tetracyclines and macrolides bind to bacterial ribosomes and stop them from making proteins. Quinolones interfere with the enzymes that copy bacterial DNA. Antibiotics do not work against viruses, such as those that cause colds and flu. When antibiotics are overused or misused, bacteria that survive can spread their resistance, which makes infections harder to treat, so they should be used only when needed.

answer: Antibiotics work by either killing bacteria or stopping them from growing. They do this by attacking things that bacteria have but human cells do not, so they don't harm the person taking them.

top.text: Jargon, or technical language, is the specialized terminology associated with a particular field or area of activity. Jargon is normally employed in a particular communicative context and may not be well understood outside that context. The context is usually a particular occupation (that is, a certain trade, profession, vernacular or academic field), but any ingroup can have jargon. The key characteristic that distinguishes jargon from the rest of a language is its specialized vocabulary, which includes terms and definitions of words that are unique to the context, and terms used in a narrower and more exact sense than when used in colloquial language. This can lead outgroups to misunderstand communication attempts. Jargon is sometimes understood as a form of technical slang and then distinguished from the official terminology used in a particular field of activity.

history.answer: A blockchain is a shared digital ledger that records transactions in blocks linked together in a chain. Each block contains a list of transactions, a timestamp and a cryptographic hash of the previous block, so changing an old block would change every block after it. Copies of the ledger are kept by many computers, called nodes, in a peer-to-peer network rather than by one central authority. The nodes agree on which new blocks to add using a consensus method such as proof of work or proof of stake. This makes the record hard to tamper with. Blockchains were first used for the cryptocurrency Bitcoin in 2009 and are also used for other cryptocurrencies, smart contracts and some supply-chain tracking.

answer: Volcanic eruptions occur when material is expelled from a volcanic vent or fissure[1]. The main mechanisms are gas release under decompression, which drives magmatic eruptions; ejection of entrained particles during steam eruptions, causing phreatic eruptions; and thermal contraction from chilling on contact with water, causing phreatomagmatic eruptions[2]. Magmatic eruptions are driven primarily by gas release due to decompression; low-viscosity magma with little dissolved gas produces gentle effusive eruptions, while high-viscosity, gas-rich magma leads to more explosive eruptions[3][4]. The style of an eruption depends on the lava's composition and viscosity, which are determined by the amount of silica and dissolved gas in the magma[4].

top.text: Magmatic eruptions are driven primarily by gas release due to decompression. Low-viscosity magma with little dissolved gas produces relatively gentle effusive eruptions. High-viscosity magma with a high content of dissolved gas produces violent explosive eruptions. The range of observed eruption styles is expressed from historical examples. Hawaiian eruptions are typical of volcanoes that erupt mafic lava with a relatively low gas content. These are almost entirely effusive, producing local lava fountains and highly fluid lava flows but relatively little tephra. They are named after the Hawaiian volcanoes. The eruption column from these eruptions does not exceed 2 km (1 mi) in height. Strombolian eruptions are characterized by moderate viscosities and dissolved gas levels. They are characterized by frequent but short-lived eruptions that can produce eruptive columns hundreds of meters high, which can also be seen in a gas slug. Their primary product is scoria. They are named after Stromboli.

sources.text: The form and style of an eruption of a volcano is largely determined by the composition of the lava it erupts. The viscosity (how fluid the lava is) and the amount of dissolved gas are the most important characteristics of magma, and both are largely determined by the amount of silica in the magma. Magma rich in silica is much more viscous than silica-poor magma, and silica-rich magma also tends to contain more dissolved gases.

sources.text: Volcanoes are formed when a plate is pushed below another plate, or at a mid-ocean ridge or hotspot. At a depth of around 100 km (62 mi), melting occurs in rock above the slab (due to the addition of water), and forms magma that reaches the surface. When the magma reaches the surface, it often builds a volcanic mountain, such as a shield volcano or a stratovolcano. Examples of volcanoes include Mount Fuji in Japan and Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines.

top.text: The speed of sound is the distance travelled per unit of time by a sound wave as it propagates through an elastic medium. More simply, the speed of sound is how fast vibrations travel. At 20 °C (68 °F), the speed of sound in air is about 343 m/s, or 1 km in 2.92 s or one mile in 4.69 s. It depends strongly on temperature as well as the medium through which a sound wave is propagating. At 0 °C (32 °F), the speed of sound in dry air (sea level 14.7 psi) is about 331 m/s. The speed of sound in an ideal gas depends only on its temperature and composition. The speed has a weak dependence on frequency and pressure in dry air, deviating slightly from ideal behavior.

history.answer: Photosynthesis is the biological process by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, convert sunlight into chemical energy. This process uses light energy to drive the reduction of carbon dioxide into carbohydrates, while releasing oxygen as a byproduct[1][3]. The main site of photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplasts of plant cells, where water is split and carbon dioxide is fixed into sugars using the energy carriers ATP and NADPH[4].

Solar panels work by converting sunlight directly into electricity using the photovoltaic effect. A typical solar panel system consists of one or more solar panels, an inverter that converts direct current (DC) electricity to alternating current (AC), and sometimes other components like charge controllers or meters[1][2]. The photovoltaic effect is the transformation of light into electrical energy, where photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly to DC electricity, which can then be converted to AC if needed[4].

The manufacturing specifications for solar panels are obtained under standard conditions, but the panels are usually exposed to different operating conditions on the installation site[3]. Solar panels are usually arranged in groups called arrays or systems, and most panels are found in solar farms or rooftop installations that supply the electricity grid[1].

top.text:
A solar panel is a device that converts sunlight into electricity by using multiple solar modules that consist of photovoltaic (PV) cells. PV cells are made of materials that produce excited electrons when exposed to light. These electrons flow through a circuit and produce direct current electricity, which can be used to power various devices or be stored in batteries. Solar panels can be known as solar cell panels, or solar electric panels.
Solar panels are usually arranged in groups called arrays or systems. A photovoltaic system consists of one or more solar panels, an inverter that converts direct current electricity to alternating current where it is necessary, and sometimes other components such as charge controllers, meters, or solar trackers to maximize direct sunlight. Most panels are in solar farms or rooftop solar panels, which supply the electricity grid.
Solar panels use a renewable and clean source of energy, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions compared to hydrocarbon-sourced energy. However, they depend on the availability and intensity of sunlight, require cleaning, and have high initial costs. Solar panels are widely used for residential, commercial, and industrial purposes, as well as in space, often together with batteries.

answer: Submarines dive by using diving planes and changing the amount of water and air in ballast tanks to affect their buoyancy[1][2]. To dive, the tanks are opened to allow air to exhaust out the top of the tanks, while seawater flows in from the bottom. Once the weight is balanced so the overall density of the submarine equals the water around it, it has neutral buoyancy and remains at that depth[2]. A crash dive is a maneuver in which the vessel submerges as quickly as possible to avoid attack[4].

top.text: Most large submarines consist of a cylindrical body with hemispherical (or conical) ends and a vertical structure, usually located amidships, which houses communications and sensing devices as well as periscopes. In modern submarines, this structure is called the "sail" in American usage and "fin" in European usage. A feature of earlier designs was the "conning tower": a separate pressure hull above the main body of the boat that enabled the use of shorter periscopes. There is a propeller (or pump jet) at the rear, and various hydrodynamic control fins. Smaller, deep-diving, and specialty submarines may deviate significantly from this traditional design. Submarines dive and resurface by using diving planes and by changing the amount of water and air in ballast tanks to affect their buoyancy.

sources.text: Submarines submerge by filling large ballast tanks with seawater. sources.text: A submarine (often shortened to sub) is a watercraft capable of independent operation underwater. … (such as the midget submarine and the wet sub). Submarines are referred to as boats rather than ships regardless of their size. Although experimental submarines had been built earlier, submarine design took off during the 19th century, and submarines were adopted by several navies.

sources.title: Crash dive
sources.text: A crash dive is a maneuver by a submarine in which the vessel submerges as quickly as possible to avoid attack. Crash diving from the surface to avoid attack has been largely rendered obsolete with the advent of nuclear-powered submarines, as they normally operate submerged. However, the crash dive is also a standard maneuver to avoid a collision.
